full_text:
Zachariah Branch had 81 receptions for 811 yards and six touchdowns in his final season at Georgia. Todd Kirkland / Getty Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — When Zachariah Branch bench-pressed 225 pounds 20 times at the NFL Combine in February, he was angry.
It didn’t matter to him that it was the fourth-highest total of any wide receiver at the event. Or that he was the lightest player (177 pounds) there to hit that mark. Or that it was as many as multiple linebackers and at least two linemen.
“I wanted to get around 24, 25,” he said. “Twenty was my minimum number.”
Branch’s expectations for himself have been high for a long time — at least since seventh grade. It was then that his father, Sheva, pulled him and his brother, Zion Branch, out of public school and homeschooled them for two years so the boys could join him in a daily workout regimen that would have been intense at any age.
“That’s when I really got locked in,” Branch said.
On most days, the Branch boys were up at 5 a.m. and in the gym by 6 with Sheva, a former San Jose State football player who is now a real estate agent and part-time conditioning coach. (Zion is a senior safety at Georgia.)
“Everybody knows if we’re going to train with my dad, it’s real work,” Zachariah said. “You better get your mind right. I definitely think it helped me out.”
Sheva had Zachariah sign a contract agreeing to drink at least two protein shakes each day to make sure he gained weight. The punishment for failure was push-ups. The reward?
“The reward was transforming my body,” the 22-year-old said.
That work — and good genes, he’s the great-nephew of Hall of Fame wide receiver Cliff Branch — started Branch down a star-studded road that led to him becoming a third-round pick of the Atlanta Falcons this year and put him on the doorstep of a starting job as a rookie.
The 5-foot-9 Branch has power-cleaned 300 pounds and squatted 500 pounds, numbers that would make much bigger men marvel. After two years of homeschooling, he enrolled at powerhouse Bishop Gorman High School in his native Las Vegas, where he was teammates with current Bears wide receiver Rome Odunze, was named the Gatorade track athlete of the year for Nevada and won two state titles in football.
From there, he went to the University of Southern California , where he met current Falcons teammate and fellow Trojan Drake London during the recruiting process and played with current Bears quarterback Caleb Williams for one year.
“I’m just excited for him,” London said of Branch. “The world is going to see.”
A speedy catch-and-run receiver who can do more than he was asked to — but how much more?
After two years at USC, Branch spent one season at Georgia, where he caught an SEC-high 81 passes for 811 yards before entering the NFL Draft. Branch was the 12th wide receiver selected this spring, falling to the third round (despite a 4.35-second 40-yard dash) because of concerns about his height and the fact that he caught almost exclusively short and screen passes in his final year of college.
If the Falcons had any concerns about Branch’s size or versatility, they were erased when Branch visited their facility before the draft.
“Zachariah is wired the right way,” Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski said. “He’s somebody that really puts in the effort on a day-to-day basis. Really that’s no surprise because that’s what (Georgia head coach Kirby Smart) told me, that’s what all his coaches told me. You watch him in practice, and he goes and he goes and he goes. He’s got the right makeup for what we want to be.”
Branch was a standout in Atlanta from the moment he stepped on the practice field for offseason workouts, and that has continued into training camp. He made a spectacular one-handed touchdown catch on a long pass during the team’s first fully padded practice Monday.
“He’s going to be a really good football player in the NFL,” said quarterback Michael Penix Jr., who threw that pass. “You already know what he’s done in college, and it’s definitely carrying over. He can really play football.”
Branch reminds Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa of former Dolphins (now Broncos) receiver Jaylen Waddle — and for more reasons than the No. 17 jersey both players wear.
“I mean, dude’s fast, very shifty,” Tagovailoa said. “Great kid, got a good head on his shoulders and he asks a lot of questions. I think that’s something very good that you like to see from rookies.”
Waddle caught 305 passes for 4,290 yards and 26 touchdowns in games Tagovailoa started for Miami, where they were teammates from 2021 to 2025.
“You find (Branch), he’s open,” Tagovailoa said. “He’s fast, and he can get away from guys. Great separation, great hands and great elusiveness when the ball is in his hands.”
The Falcons plan to line up Branch at all three wide receiver spots, but his quickest path to playing time is probably the F (slot) position where veteran Olamide Zaccheaus is still taking most of the first-team snaps. Branch is looming, though, and everyone in Atlanta can see it.
“He’s a little joystick man,” Zaccheaus said. “He has different movement than a lot of people in the league. There’s little things I can teach him, but he has a great understanding of how to run routes.”
For now, Branch is focusing only on each day.
“I like to get coached hard,” he said. “I am kind of a perfectionist. If I did make a mistake, I want to make sure that’s the last time I make that mistake and not be a repeat offender. My mindset is definitely just to keep getting 1 percent better every day.”

full_text:
Joe Brady and Josh Allen hope to knock down the proverbial wall en route to the Super Bowl this season. Bryan Bennett / Getty Images
The obvious connection between New Orleans and Buffalo dates back more than 60 years.
As popular — but perhaps not entirely true — legend has it, Buffalo wings were invented at the Anchor Bar in 1964, when the owner doused some chicken parts with Frank’s RedHot Sauce and served them up with celery and a side of bleu cheese dressing.
This offseason, the Buffalo Bills decided to cook up another north-south collaboration.
And they laid it on thick.
Since the day the Bills named Joe Brady head coach, they have promoted his relationships with former New Orleans Saints coach Sean Payton and quarterback Drew Brees, who will be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday.
“I got a master’s degree at Penn State, but I got a doctorate in New Orleans,” was a line Brady said the day he was introduced as the Bills’ new head coach and which he repeated often along the national media circuit.
While finishing his master’s degree in educational leadership at Penn State, Brady entered the NFL as a Saints offensive assistant in 2017 and 2018 before joining LSU’s staff as passing game coordinator and helping the Tigers win the 2019 national championship. It was a solid curriculum vitae for the NFL’s youngest head coach.
But would it be good enough for Buffalo to recreate New Orleans’ syllabus?
Brees was a deity in New Orleans, and by the time he retired, he held the NFL record for career passing yards and ranked second in touchdown passes and completion percentage. Yet during Brees’ 15 years there, New Orleans won only one Super Bowl (2009). It never returned to the big game, and failed to make the postseason six times.
The club had so much money committed to its franchise quarterback that it struggled to assemble a comprehensive roster. The Saints went 7-9 four times during a five-year span in which Brees led the NFL in passing yards four times, averaging 5,074 yards and 37 TDs per season.
Then again, maybe a single Lombardi Trophy would satisfy Bills fans.
Bobby Hebert didn’t take the classes, but he knows all the professors and has dissected the lessons.
“Under Drew Brees and Sean Payton, they should have won or gone to at least three Super Bowls,” said Hebert, the legendary Saints quarterback from Cut Off, La.
“I guess you can say they underachieved. It just goes to show how hard it is to win the Super Bowl, the ultimate. The Bills better take advantage of Josh Allen.”
Early this offseason, Brady repeatedly mentioned being “from the Sean Payton tree.” The comment entered a pantheon of “Hey, did you know” jokes among local reporters alongside former Bills overachievers Ryan Fitzpatrick attending Harvard and Chris Hogan starting out as a lacrosse player.
“Look, I was a coaching assistant, right?” Brady said. “I was bottom of the barrel, sleeping at the office, loving life. But I got an opportunity to learn everything from him, and there’s no way in hell I’d be sitting in this chair right now if I didn’t get that opportunity to be his coaching assistant.”
Brady said he’s going to keep calling plays because he has seen Payton be successful at it. Brady hired two coordinators away from Payton, who has been the Denver Broncos’ coach since 2023. The first was offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael, who also spent 14 seasons with Payton and the Saints, followed by defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Brady’s senior adviser, former head coach John Fox, was the New York Giants’ defensive coordinator in 2001 and 2002 when Payton was their offensive coordinator.
“But the biggest thing that I learned along the way,” said Brady, “is that if I’m not myself, it’s not going to work. If I try to just, hey, pick up, ‘Oh, this is what Coach Payton did’ and take it somewhere else, that’s not going to work. That’s important, that I have to be me, and I think the great coaches that I’ve been around have been comfortable in who they are.”
Brady made an impression on Brees, who said he “wasn’t surprised” when Brady left New Orleans and won a national title on LSU’s staff, working with future NFL stars Joe Burrow, Justin Jefferson and Ja’Marr Chase. After that amazing season, at just 30 years old, Brady began interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs.
“I think his demeanor, his personality is one that, as a quarterback, you really feel like you can relate to him,” Brees said. “He’s really built the system around the guys that he has. He’s going to be able to do a lot of creative, innovative stuff there.
“Sean was brilliant in so many ways. He was brilliant in the way he narrowed the focus for the team week in and week out. He was brilliant in the way that he managed the coaching staff and helped develop his coaches to go on and be play callers and head coaches elsewhere. A lot of guys who have coached under Sean Payton would give him a lot of credit for a lot of things and say they learned a whole lot.
“And, back in those days, Joe Brady probably was supporting Pete Carmichael in ways that he is probably now supporting Joe.”
Hebert knew Brady way back when.
Hebert, who turns 66 this month, remains a New Orleans fixture. He has been immersed in Saints and LSU football as a sportscaster there for 25 years. His Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame bio calls him “the most successful quarterback in team history,” greater than Saints icon Archie Manning, until Brees came along. Hebert was born on the bayou. He was a state-championship high school teammate and Northwestern State roommate with — and is a cousin of — Brady’s LSU boss, Ed Orgeron.
“People don’t realize: Joe Brady gets a lot of credit, but he wasn’t calling the plays,” Hebert said. “Brady had a lot of input, but Steve Ensminger was the one really running that LSU offense when they were having the greatest season ever in college football.
“What Joe Brady would do is help out Ensminger in the red zone and with certain plays and on third down. Ensminger would, for Brady to get his feet wet, let him call a few series. But Ensminger is a humble man, so he doesn’t demand the credit he deserves.”
That said, Hebert predicted Brady will prove to be a good hire for Buffalo. The “Cajun Cannon” noted that Brady’s learning curve was aided by a disappointing-but-educational stint as the Carolina Panthers’ offensive coordinator and then by his re-emergence with Allen and the Bills. Hebert said he sees many positive similarities between Brady and young Saints coach Kellen Moore.
As for any Saints redux, Hebert avoided that nasty NFL voodoo.
“The year they won the Super Bowl, that wasn’t even the Saints’ best team,” Hebert said. “The best team was in 2011. They became the new Greatest Show on Turf, better than those Rams teams. They were No. 1 in a number of offensive categories.”
That Saints team was upset by the San Francisco 49ers in the second round. New Orleans surrendered a 17-point lead in the second quarter and committed five turnovers, but took a pair of leads within the final five minutes, the last with 1:37 left. They didn’t survive.
Then, there was the “NOLA No-Call” at the end of the 2018 NFC Championship Game.
“Look at Dan Marino: ‘Oh, he’s just a rookie, he’ll be back.’ Look at Joe Burrow, who got there and lost and now might never get back,” Hebert said. “It’s hard.”
Despite having an all-time great at the most critical position for 15 years, the Saints’ front office struggled infamously with the salary cap, frequently cutting serviceable veterans and constantly restructuring contracts to comply. When they signed Bills left guard David Edwards in March for $61 million over four years, stunned media and fans noted the deal included no void years , ubiquitous since long before Brees retired after the 2020 season.

full_text:
The Panthers surround Haynes King after the undrafted rookie quarterback scored the game-winning touchdown as time expired Thursday night. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
CANTON, Ohio — It wasn’t necessarily the kind of game Luke Kuechly would have loved as a player: an offensive shootout with a couple of over-the-top plays surrendered by the Carolina Panthers defense.
The good news is the Panthers won Thursday, kicking off Kuechly’s Hall of Fame weekend with a 33-30 victory over the Arizona Cardinals when rookie quarterback Haynes King walked it off with a 5-yard touchdown scramble as time expired at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium.
“That was a lot of fun!” Panthers coach Dave Canales exclaimed. “Haynes did a fantastic job just keeping the play alive, whatever he had to do — run it, throw it, doesn’t matter. Move the chains and keep it alive.”
The Panthers defense made Cardinals rookie Carson Beck look like one of the quarterbacks whose bronze busts are displayed next door at the Pro Football Hall of Fame. The former Georgia and Miami QB torched the second- and third-stringers in the secondary for a Dan Marino-like stat line: 15-of-19 for 188 yards and a touchdown, with a passer rating of 125.4.
But King had the ball last and avenged an eight-overtime loss to Beck at Georgia in 2024 as Georgia Tech’s quarterback.
A look at the winners and losers from the Panthers’ first exhibition game:
The undrafted free agent replaced Kenny Pickett in the second quarter and proceeded to lead scoring drives on five of his six series. He was composed in the pocket, made plays with his feet and looked like a guy who’s going to be on a 53-man roster this year. It’ll be hard for Dan Morgan to try to stash King on the practice squad.
“I’m very excited that I got this opportunity. I feel like I went out there and operated at a high level,” said King, who completed 21 of 34 passes for 180 yards and added 39 rushing yards. “And I feel like I affected a lot of people and allowed everybody around me to play better as well.”
Rookie Chris Brazzell’s season-ending knee injury opened the door for several of the Panthers’ other receivers, three of whom — whose first names happen to begin with J — had solid showings.
Ja’seem Reed built on his promising training camp by scoring on a 15-yard touchdown pass from King in the first half and finishing with two receptions for 30 yards. Jimmy Horn Jr. had four catches for 44 yards, with a long of 17.
John Metchie III pulled down three passes for 38 yards to go with a 36-yard kick return, which helped kick-start his night. “I think it helps momentum. I think it helps a bunch of things,” he said. “That one, it was just my first time running, so I got warm after that.”
Lathan Ransom and Zakee Wheatley, who are competing for the No. 3 safety spot, helped themselves in Canton. “Our safeties showed up,” Canales said.
Ransom, the former Ohio State standout, made big plays on defense and special teams. The fourth-round pick from 2025 downed a punt inside the 5-yard line in the second quarter when the Cardinals returner failed to field it. (There was a lot of that going around Thursday night.) Later in the first half, Ransom rocked Jalen Brooks after the Cardinals receiver had gotten behind Akayleb Evans (more on that in a bit).
Wheatley, the rookie from Penn State, led all tacklers with eight stops and forced a fumble the Cardinals recovered.
Wallace didn’t necessarily play poorly. It’s the fact he played at all that could be viewed as a little disconcerting. Canales said any starter-level players in uniform are still battling for a starting job. That means Wallace, who started 20 games at inside linebacker his first two seasons, hasn’t secured the spot alongside Devin Lloyd.
Call Thursday a draw between Wallace (three assisted tackles) and veteran Claudin Cherelus, who finished with four tackles (two solo, two assists).
It was a rough night for several of the cornerbacks vying for the reserve spots behind Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, who were on the sidelines in street clothes. Rookie Will Lee, the fourth-round pick from Texas A&M who’s had a productive start to camp, endured an up-and-down first quarter: He had a nice pass breakup (for a long time, it was Beck’s only incompletion), was beaten on a double move by Brooks for a 35-yard reception, and bounced back to make a nifty open-field tackle.
In the second quarter, the veteran Evans, who started opposite Lee, was whistled for an illegal contact penalty against Brooks. Evans didn’t hold him well enough, though: Brooks burned him on a stop-and-go for a 49-yard pickup.
That was the big play on a drive Beck capped by feathering a 5-yard touchdown pass to Simi Fehoko, who beat Corey Thornton to the pylon.
“We’ve gotta stay on top. You’ve gotta own the deep ball. We had to be there,” Canales said. “The safeties were in position. The corners gotta make plays out there on the perimeter, and everything else was pretty solid.”
The second-year running back/return specialist let the Cardinals’ first punt hit and roll, burying Pickett and the offense at their own 3-yard line for their second series. On the ensuing play, Etienne was dropped for a 2-yard loss. The Panthers escaped the poor starting position thanks to a pass interference penalty. Etienne (four carries, 12 yards) never got going in the run game, although there weren’t many holes when he was in the game.

full_text:
Caleb Williams landed in Tier 2 of Mike Sando's Quarterback Tiers this year, a first for a Bears quarterback. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
What a strange week this had to be for Chicago Bears fans amid the annual summer exercise of surveying exactly how the rest of the league feels about their starting quarterback.
Mike Sando’s always illuminating and intel-filled “Quarterback Tiers” launched Tuesday at The Athletic. In Chicago, there was much less scrolling than ever before, the “page down” function spared on many laptops.
Yes, here indeed was Caleb Williams on the rise. From Tier 3 last season up into Tier 2, with a year-over-year jump of 12 pegs to No. 11 overall.
That’s another sign of the times, with the Bears offense, led by its talented 24-year-old quarterback, generating significant buzz around the NFL.
“I’ve got all these cutups on him, and I’m going, ‘This guy is special.’ He makes unbelievable throws, and he’s fearless,” one head coach told Sando. Like the others quoted, he spoke on condition of anonymity to share a candid evaluation.
So what does it all mean? It’s enough to get the wheels turning.
Sando began doing this project in 2014. His inaugural list had Jay Cutler — heading into his second season working with Bears coach Marc Trestman — in Tier 3 and at No. 17 overall, sandwiched between Cam Newton of the Panthers and Alex Smith of the Chiefs.
Over the following 10 seasons, five other Bears quarterbacks were part of the project. Mike Glennon, Mitch Trubisky, Nick Foles, Andy Dalton and Justin Fields. Their average ranking: No. 25. Average tier: 3.5. Smack dab in the middle of mediocrity.
So, yes, in a small way, the current assessment of Williams in league circles qualifies as a breakthrough. In Sando’s survey, no Bears quarterback had ever been in Tier 2 before. None had ever been viewed as a top-15 guy either.
“He is an exciting player, definitely athletic,” a defensive coordinator said. “The good thing for him, just like Lamar (Jackson) and Josh (Allen) at this stage: It doesn’t look like the moment is too big for him.”
For the record, the thumbnail criteria for a Tier 2 quarterback in Sando’s exercise are as follows.
Fair. That description fits.
Williams’ ability to carry his team has been on display. In big moments and in big games. But he also has identifiable flaws, with some around the league expressing at least some concern about his habits of playing off-schedule too often, which contributes to his inconsistency. Those evaluations marry up with the ongoing push at Halas Hall for Williams to improve his completion percentage and ball location.
And if Bears coach Ben Johnson needs more motivational material to slide onto Williams’ chair, he can point to the quarterbacks immediately ahead of Williams in Tier 2. Johnson’s former quarterback in Detroit (Jared Goff) is at No. 8, tied with Drake Maye, who entered the league in the same 2024 draft class as Williams. And the fella whom nemesis Matt LaFleur coaches in Green Bay (Jordan Love) sits right there at No. 10. All three are on the Bears’ schedule this season.
The hope in Chicago is that on most game days Williams will walk into the stadium as the best quarterback there and leave as that day’s most productive. To that end, of the 14 opponents on the schedule this season, only one features a Tier 1 quarterback: Buffalo’s Josh Allen. Beyond that, the Bears are scheduled to face seven starting quarterbacks from Tier 2, two from Tier 3 and two from Tier 4.
That doesn’t include the future winners of quarterback competitions in Atlanta — Tua Tagovailoa (Tier 3) vs. Michael Penix Jr. (Tier 4) — and Minnesota — Kyler Murray (Tier 3) vs. J.J. McCarthy (Tier 4).
Williams’ investment in the grind will remain a big deal as he climbs toward the summit of Tier 1, which this year features only four elite quarterbacks: Patrick Mahomes, Allen, Matthew Stafford and Joe Burrow.
Johnson’s ability to teach his quarterback and push his buttons will also factor in.
Right now, the Johnson-Williams union is as strong as ever. As running back D’Andre Swift noted this week, “For one, it’s the love of the game they both have. Ben expects nothing but greatness out of everybody and doesn’t let you slack. I think that’s something Caleb gravitates to.”
Specifically, I’ve been thinking about the direction being provided at Halas Hall — by Johnson and his staff of driven assistants — and why it continues to resonate.
For more than a year, there has been a drumbeat of praise coming out of the locker room about how well this coaching staff communicates and how well the individuals lead. The buy-in is undeniable. And with each passing week, a new testimonial seems to surface.
One of the most recent came from right tackle Darnell Wright, who signed a four-year, $116 million extension Tuesday, then spent part of his Wednesday explaining some of the keys that helped unlock this new world.
Just a year ago, Wright was a third-year player seeking guidance and being challenged by Johnson and offensive line coach Dan Roushar to up his intensity as well as his understanding of what was being asked of him. Now, as the highest-paid right tackle in football, Wright has gratitude for the push both men gave.
With Johnson, Wright said, all the coaching has been backed by purpose, with the Bears coach offering his right tackle confidence-building reminders of how important he is.
“When he first got here, he instilled the confidence into me that I was going to be a (major) part of the offense,” Wright said. “I’ve never had a coach really come up to me and be like, ‘We’re depending on you.’ Obviously you do your job. But (with him), it’s ‘We’re depending on you to complete this play. This is pretty much your play.'”
With Roushar, Wright has appreciated and been fueled by constant constructive criticism. “He’s hard to please,” Wright said.
Still, there wasn’t an ounce of aggravation in that observation because the connection Roushar initially established came with trust that he was a) working to bring out Wright’s best and b) on point with his instruction.
“He is such a good teacher,” Wright said. “And he does it with such good (delivery). He’s not yelling at you, he’s not screaming at you, he’s not demeaning you. He’s telling you what’s good about the rep and he’s telling you what’s bad about the rep so you can see both sides.”
For Wright, it’s all been refreshing.
“I just don’t vibe well with a coach who’s just (loud),” he said. “You can yell until your lungs go out. But there has to be some substance in what you’re saying. As long as there’s substance, you can yell as much as you want. Just have something to teach about.”
During these early stages of camp, the ground game is beginning to come to life, with the Bears confident they will get off to a quicker start in that department this season. Last year, in Johnson’s first season, the Bears stumbled into their Week 5 bye still trying to discover what worked best and working for greater synergy with the rushing attack. Through the first four games, they ranked 24th in the league in rushing (102.3 yards per game) before getting rolling and ultimately finishing third at 144.5 yards per game.
Big outings in Cincinnati (283) and Philadelphia (281) certainly helped, pieces of the evidence that further established Johnson as a running game devotee — and a bit of a visionary in that department.
Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen took his stab this week at explaining how Johnson gets it all started.
“He does a good job with trying to create the formations and the angles in the blocking scheme to try to gain the advantage on the defense,” Allen said. “I think they do a good job mixing in zone schemes with gap schemes. And then their ability to give you the same look and then have play-action pass off of it (is impressive).”
Swift, fresh off a 1,087-yard, nine-touchdown rushing season, also highlighted the multiplicity of the Bears’ running game, noting their ability to strain…

full_text:

CINCINNATI — The Cincinnati Bengals have completed three padded practices, and the success enjoyed by the defense continues to be the storyline of camp.
The potent Cincinnati offense struggled to find a rhythm or explosiveness, but nobody is hitting the concern alarm on Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins just yet. And though nobody will be putting the Bengals defense in the same conversation as the 1985 Chicago Bears anytime soon, early returns are undeniably encouraging.
Though the defense’s strong foundation offers a broad-brush view of camp’s most important storyline, there have been individual successes within that unit providing optimism beyond the big names.
Here’s a look at four players who’ve made early splashes and why these results can plant seeds for a critical development once the season begins.
The second-round pick out of Texas A&M won SEC Defensive Player of the Year, so making a good first impression in Cincinnati isn’t a surprise. What he did to Orlando Brown on Thursday was.
Howell enjoyed success going against second-teamers through the first week of practices. Thursday’s reps turned toward defensive packages that feature him with the starters and were a reward of opportunity given what he’s shown.
In his first rep against the starting left tackle, Howell got under his chin, drove the 6-8, 350-pound veteran backward and eventually planted him on his back at Burrow’s feet.
Howell earned his reputation with speed, burst and bend for the Aggies, so to show off that level of power was an eye-opener.
“He’s been really physical,” coach Zac Taylor said. “He’s really embraced the physicality of playing defensive end. That’s a great starting point for a rookie, where he’s not afraid to take on blocks and really strain and make some plays in the run game. He’s got natural pass-rush ability, which shows up on a daily basis. He can drive us crazy on offense because he’s really good at it.”
He drove Brown crazy by following the bull-rush rep with a teleport around the outside edge to get near Burrow’s back on a pass play soon after.
Howell was far from perfect and had his share of reps that went nowhere against other starters, but there’s no denying the early impression he’s making.
Taylor gave Howell one of the highest compliments when he compared the physicality he sees from Howell to that of tight end Erick All, whom the coach referenced earlier this year as “the word physical in the dictionary is a picture of Erick All trying to put his face through somebody’s soul.”
Howell brought that vision to life against Brown.
Flashes might deliver viral highlights, but repetition delivers playing time. If Howell can keep this rolling, he’ll have a serious role in passing situations and the outside edge rusher when the Bengals shift to a 3-4 on early downs.
“Now it’s just what’s the consistency going to look like over a 30-day training camp period?” Taylor said. “I believe we’re going to see that from him from everything I’ve known about him and seen from him. But we’ll just continue to see what just happens over the next couple of weeks.”
Johnson produced similar excitement as Howell from the same position. Really, the entire edge rusher contingent might be the most electric in camp. Boye Mafe has been a consistent winner, Myles Murphy continues to find the backfield, and the ascension of Howell and Johnson provides depth the team desires in waves.
He’s popped multiple times, bending around the edge nearly untouched, and earned a few reps against the first team as the defense rotates. Johnson’s built more like Mafe and less like the smaller Howell, but the 2024 sixth-round pick looks to be blossoming.
Johnson produced a pressure once every 7.9 pass-rush snaps last season. That ranked second among Bengals edge rushers, narrowly topped by Trey Hendrickson at 7.7.
For his career, he’s produced 23 pressures in 197 pass-rush snaps.
The flashes have been there in games; he’s merely lacked opportunity. Faith in him has only grown so far this camp, and now the defensive scheme more fits his strengths on the edge.
Cornerbacks coach Chuck Burks mentioned to Ivey on Tuesday morning that he’d be running with the first team that day. Ivey settled into the backup role through the first week of camp, but with Dax Hill battling a minor ailment, Ivey had a chance to line up against Higgins and Chase, and Hill took a rest day.
And just like that, opportunity fell in his lap. It did so again Thursday with Hill still limited during team drills.
“I’m just trying to stack days,” Ivey said. “Whatever opportunity I get — special teams, defense, third down — just go out there and try to make plays and do the best I can to help the team.”
The days are stacking after a solid first week.
Ivey has made the most of his time running with the first team, with a pass breakup on a deep post from Burrow to Higgins on Tuesday, then in perfect position to break up another deep ball for Higgins on Thursday. He hasn’t been picked on consistently or caught out of step.
In short, Ivey looked the part.
Add this to the role the Bengals already know he can play as the tight end-stopper, and confidence in him as the next cornerback up behind the starters is on the rise.
Cook wouldn’t classify as under the radar by contract or respect level. He came over from the Kansas City Chiefs after signing a three-year, $40 million contract this offseason. Cook will be counted on to stabilize a notably unstable back end of the defense in 2025.
He’s done that in quieter ways through the early portion of camp, noted more for his communication and leadership from the safety position than any specific plays he made.
That changed Tuesday. To conclude practice, Cook stepped in front of a Burrow pass, beating receiver Mitchell Tinsley to the spot of an anticipation throw. He snagged an interception and raced the other way for a touchdown.
The lack of blown assignments has been notable in the early going, and Cook deserves a significant amount of credit for that.
His fellow safety Jordan Battle, specifically, noted the difference as he’s started getting used to playing next to Cook.
“He’s dedicated to winning, you could tell,” Battle said. “Just the first day coming in, asking a lot of questions, making sure guys are comfortable before they go on the field. Making sure things are easy for us so we can just go out there and play.”
Having his presence and communication make such a quick transition in the early portion of camp is an encouraging sign for shoring up the back line of the defense with several new players in the mix.

title: 'Loud in a good way': Brian Schottenheimer can't help but notice Cowboys' defense First-time DC Christian Parker has the defense performing well, but the first big test comes next week in a joint practice with the Rams. Jon Machota

First-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker is putting his stamp on his new group. The communication issues of a year ago are unlikely to be r
full_text:
Dallas coach Brian Schottenheimer, right, likes what he's seeing from new defensive coordinator Christian Parker, left, so far in training camp. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
OXNARD, Calif. — The sounds are a little different this year around the Dallas Cowboys’ training camp facility. It’s not difficult to find the defensive meeting room during the day.
First-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker is putting his stamp on his new group. The communication issues of a year ago are unlikely to be repeated this coming season.
While the constant talking pre-snap is noticeable during practice, the 34-year-old Parker has the group using that same intensity when they’re preparing off the field. And the decibel level sometimes gets so loud that it impacts what others are doing nearby.
“It felt like playing on the road,” Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said of a recent offensive meeting. “We were just trying to install our (offense) and it was loud and intense. That’s contagious. You feel that on that side of the ball. That unit is giving you that, you want to do the same on offense. Nothing but good things to say about that unit.”
Parker wants his players to be trained to talk the same whether it’s a game, practice or meeting.
“If we’re showing a play from practice, for example, if you’re a linebacker on the field, you’re making the front adjustment,” Parker explained. “If you’re an outside linebacker and you see that the Y is off, you’re saying something to your partner. If I’m a DB, I’m calling out the coverage communication. Motion happens. We’re alerting this, we’re passing off this. Once the play starts, what is that communication?
“We want the meeting room to sound the same as it does on the field. Your brain doesn’t know when you’re not taking a physical rep. It just knows that your brain is strained. So as many reps that we can get on task on that is possible, we want to try to take advantage of those in that space.”
Cowboys coach and offensive play caller Brian Schottenheimer has been working in the NFL for over 25 years. Parker’s way of teaching communication “jumps out” to him.
“It’s loud in a good way,” Schottenheimer said. “There’s a lot of communication. I love what he says and how he refers to it as it’s two parts, giving and receiving. You just can’t be blurting out a bunch of stuff that doesn’t matter and confusing people. You got to give it, you got to receive it.
“And then there’s the nonverbal part, which I think that’s the thing that has probably caught me the most. We all talk about communication, the importance of it, but the way the defensive staff talks about is there’s no audio on the practice film. So therefore the visual hand signals of things are critical because otherwise you can say, ‘Yeah, I said it.’ But if you don’t visually give the signal, then how do we know if you said it when the music’s playing stuff? I think it’s really, really cool how they preach that.”
Parker understands that someone walking by their meeting room might think something is wrong. He says that’s a good thing.
“I can’t just be aimlessly yelling and saying a bunch of things if I don’t know who I’m talking to,” he said, “what those words mean, how that changes things, when we can adjust something, when we can’t. … We still have more to go, but there’s a lot of encouraging things that are happening from a vocal standpoint.”
Parker is taking over a mess. The 2025 Cowboys were probably the worst defense in franchise history. Trading superstar pass rusher Micah Parsons a week before the season started obviously didn’t help. They’ve made moves to improve the defensive roster, and they’re likely not done.
It would not be surprising to see Dallas add another edge rusher or inside linebacker before Week 1. But it remains to be seen if those additions could be as impactful as trading for an elite pass rusher such as Maxx Crosby or potentially signing 37-year-old Von Miller, MVP of Super Bowl 50.
If the season started this weekend, the defensive starters would likely be Rashan Gary and Donovan Ezeiruaku at outside linebacker/edge rushers, Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark as the interior defensive linemen, DeMarvion Overshown and Dee Winters at inside linebacker, DaRon Bland and Cobie Durant at outside cornerback, Caleb Downs at nickel cornerback and Jalen Thompson and Malik Hooker at safety.
Regardless of that being the starting group or potential future upgrades, Parker appears to be laying a quality foundation.
“I think the first thing is we want to be detailed in our work and our fundamentals and technique and obviously the mastery of the scheme,” he said Wednesday. “But there’s an element of violence and physicality that we want to play with that we will play with. So I think it’s just kind of tying all those things together in terms of knowing your job, knowing what the man next to you is doing, who you are connected to, are you on an island on that certain play? And then doing that with an attitude and the physicality required to play this game.”
It’s difficult to project how much improvement the defense will display this season. It has played well in training camp since full pads came on Monday. But last year’s defense had good days at camp, too.
We’ll get a much better idea Tuesday when the Cowboys travel roughly 40 miles east to the Los Angeles Rams’ practice facility for a joint practice. Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, didn’t even participate in the teams’ joint practice last year and the Rams still did whatever they wanted on offense.
“I think it’s real important, especially as much experience as Coach (Sean) McVay has and Matthew Stafford at that position,” Parker said. “The pre-snap looks and the motions and the things they do formationally. They’ve been a very successful offense during his tenure there. So it’s going to be a good test for us of where we’re at and make sure our eyes are right and we’re playing with the right demeanor.”
Parker is expected to call the defense during that practice as he has been during all camp practices, from the sideline on a handheld radio. It’s still to be determined if he will call the defense this season from the sideline or from the coaching booth. Schottenheimer said Thursday that “in a perfect world, he’ll be down” on the sideline.
Parker isn’t one to heap significant praise on anything that’s happening in camp practices. Things appear to be moving in the right direction. But he knows the defense and his first year on the job will be judged by the results on Sunday.
His views on that seem to line up with his response to a recent question about whether there are players he thinks have a similar leadership style as he does.
“We’ll wait to answer that,” Parker said. “We haven’t been in the fire yet.”

title: Ja'Quan McMillian's playoff moment rescued the Broncos. Is a long-term deal next? "He makes the whole thing go," teammate Zach Allen said of McMillian's role in Denver's defense. Nick Kosmider
summary:

ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Sean Payton wanted to attempt a fake punt. On fourth-and-11. From his own 38-yard line. In overtime of a tie game in the divisional round of last season’s NFL playoffs. full_text:
Ja'Quan McMillian pulls the ball away from Brandin Cooks for a pivotal interception against the Bills in last season's playoffs. Matthew Stockman / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Sean Payton wanted to attempt a fake punt. On fourth-and-11. From his own 38-yard line. In overtime of a tie game in the divisional round of last season’s NFL playoffs. Stripped of further context, it sounds like an idea that borders on lunacy. Until you recall the path of the moon ball as it left Josh Allen’s arm, moments after the Broncos ultimately checked out of the fake-punt call Payton had radioed in and then booted the ball back to the Bills.
“We just wanted (a fake call), late in the game, (where) we have the lead and we aren’t able to get the first down,” Payton said as training camp began last week. “We’ve seen this script with a player (like Allen), and this is a great sign of respect for one of the elite quarterbacks in our league. … We looked at it again in this playoff game, that if we were in that position where we are punting and a field goal is going to win it, (we’d call a fake) — and, I’ll be darned, we were in that position.”
Allen effortlessly flicked his wrist to release the ball from his own 25-yard line on third-and-10. With each tick of the ball’s descent, Denver’s resurgent season appeared more doomed. Veteran Bills receiver Brandin Cooks was running under the heave, ready to help author a signature playoff moment for Allen while putting the Bills firmly into range for a winning field goal.
In that season-on-the-line moment, Broncos defensive back Ja’Quan McMillian rapidly processed what a catch by Cooks would mean. He envisioned, if subconsciously and only for a micro-second, the pain a completion would bring — and then refused to experience it.
“I had to pull something out of my … yeah, you know,” McMillian said in a quiet corner outside the Broncos’ sparkling new training facility earlier this week, a slow grin growing across his face. “As I’m falling to the ground, I knew I had to either make sure he dropped the ball or I came up with an interception. That’s what I did.”
Cooks appeared to catch the ball as it fell from the frigid sky into his hands. But as the two players tumbled to the ground, McMillian ripped the ball away before Cooks could complete the reception. McMillian made the instantly iconic play — he remains as sure it was an interception as Cooks remains sure it was a catch — because it’s what he’s always done. And soon, whether it is during this training camp, during the season or in the weeks to follow, the Broncos will have a chance to show just how much they value the clutch playmaking McMillian has displayed since entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2022.
“He always finds a way,” said Mike Houston, who coached McMillian at East Carolina University. “There’s been times where you say, ‘Ehh, I don’t know if (he’ll get to the ball),’ and then, ‘Yep, he made the play.’ So when he makes that play (against Buffalo), it doesn’t shock you. It’s who he is.”
McMillian is set to play this season on the one-year, $5.76 million restricted free agent tender he signed in March. That is already a hearty raise from the $880,000 he averaged during his first four seasons in the league, but it’s also a far cry from what he’ll command when he signs a multiyear contract at some point in the near future — be it with the Broncos or someone else.
“He’s one of our core players,” Broncos general manager George Paton said at the NFL Combine in February, “and we love having him here.”
Among corners who spend the majority of their time in the slot — McMillian led all players with a 90 percent rate of snaps in that spot in 2025 — recent extensions have ranged from $10 million in average annual value (Jacksonville’s Jourdan Lewis) to $13.3 million (Chicago’s Kyler Gordon). Given the particular importance of his role in coordinator Vance Joseph’s defense and the rising market for defensive backs in general, McMillian could well be in position to exceed those totals.
“He makes the whole thing go,” defensive end Zach Allen said earlier this week when asked about McMillian’s role in a defense that has grown into one of the league’s best the past two seasons. “The fact that he’s able to cover, blitz, the whole nine. J-Mac’s incredible. We were literally just talking about it in the locker room that we’re lucky to have him.”
It was hard to envision McMillian rising to this spot with the Broncos back in 2022, at least to outside observers. After becoming a second-team All-American with ECU as a junior in 2021, breaking up a school-record 16 passes, he decided to enter the NFL Draft. But no team was willing to chance a draft pick on a 5-foot-10, 183-pound corner who had only played on the boundary in college, so he signed with Denver on a deal that came with a $15,000 signing bonus and $75,000 in total guarantees.
Houston was disappointed not to have McMillian return for his final year of college eligibility, but he knew the young defensive back would stick in the NFL in no small part because of his innate feel for making the plays demanded in a game’s most critical moments.
“He had so many of those where he would just come up with something,” Houston said. “We were at Marshall his junior year. We were down and came back and took the lead with a minute-and-a-half to go, but then Marshall’s driving down the field. It’s inside of 30 seconds left in the game. They try a one-on-one ball in the front corner of the end zone and J-Mac picks it at the 1-yard line to win the game. We went on a four-game win streak after that win up there and that was the year we had our first winning season at ECU in almost a decade. It was a pivotal play, in crunch time, that spurred the season we had.”
McMillian’s first season as a de facto starter in the NFL in 2023 featured a similar stretch. His first interception came off Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes and helped Denver beat Kansas City for the first time since 2015. One week later, against Buffalo on “Monday Night Football,” he ripped the ball from running back James Cook on the game’s first play and recovered it, setting the tone for a Broncos upset.
It was more of the same last season. His game-clinching sack of Mahomes in Week 11 — he also intercepted him early in the game — set the Broncos on the path to their first AFC West title in a decade. When they needed to overcome a jittery start against the Chargers in Week 18, the No. 1 seed in the AFC on the line for Denver, it was McMillian who pounced on a deflected pass and returned it 45 yards for a touchdown that invited a nervous fan base to exhale.
“When I see someone who’s really good at taking the ball away, I see football IQ and someone who is playing with good leverage,” Payton said. “It’s easy to say, ‘Take it away,’ but sometimes, if you’re not in position, you’re just trying to catch up and make a tackle. I think he’s a great study.”
It would be easy to attribute McMillian’s propensity for monster takeaways to a spidey sense for the ball. After all, this is a player who, as a freshman cornerback entering West Forsyth High in North Carolina, picked off the very first pass thrown his way in his first summer 7-on-7 tournament.
“The dude,” as safety Brandon Jones put it, “just makes plays.”
Yet, to chalk it all up to some innate magnetic superpower that draws McMillian and the ball together would be to discount all that occurs behind the scenes. Cornerback Riley Moss, one of the stars of this Broncos camp who is also entering a contract year, worked with McMillian and trainer Chad Wilson in Florida this offseason for the first time. It gave Moss a greater appreciation for the intentionality with which McMillian approaches improvement.
“He’s always getting better at something,” Moss said. “When we got out to the field, it’s business first and that’s what I respect about him. That was the mentality he had during my first year here (in 2023). He had to scratch…

title: The early star of Vikings camp? CB Charles Demmings, communicator extraordinaire Demmings, a fifth-round pick out of Stephen F. Austin, has turned heads with his playmaking at Vikings training camp. Alec Lewis
summary:
Charles Demmings, a rookie cornerback out of Stephen F. Austin shown during the NFL Scouting Combine, has turned heads at Vikings training camp. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Almost 15 years ago, a group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology began studying a fascinating question: Can you identify shared traits among great teams? Furthermore, could you take those insights and reverse-engineer them for future teams?
Researchers at the school explored industries such as banks, call
full_text:
Charles Demmings, a rookie cornerback out of Stephen F. Austin shown during the NFL Scouting Combine, has turned heads at Vikings training camp. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Almost 15 years ago, a group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology began studying a fascinating question: Can you identify shared traits among great teams? Furthermore, could you take those insights and reverse-engineer them for future teams?
Researchers at the school explored industries such as banks, call centers and hospital recovery wards. They equipped workers with electronic badges that collected real-time data on communication behavior such as tone of voice and body language.
The Harvard Business Review published the results in 2012. Energy and engagement were the central takeaways.
“We now know that 35 percent of variation in a team’s performance can be accounted for simply by the number of face-to-face exchanges among team members,” the report read . “We know as well that the most efficient work was done by high-energy, high-engagement teams.”
This seemed relevant this week when, following a Charles Demmings pass deflection in the red zone, all of the Minnesota Vikings’ players pointed and laughed. Demmings held his palm to the ground, a taunt to suggest that the receiver is too small . Even wide receivers coach Keenan McCardell smirked.
The monotony of training camp makes joy in these moments almost a necessity. Demmings drops it in abundance.
Before practice each day, he trots out to the TCO Performance Center practice fields and gives the cameras some words of wisdom. After conversations, he extends a hand and says something to the effect of: “Keep being a gift to the world.”
Even during down days, keeping the vibe positive matters. It has already earned Demmings praise from teammates such as veteran cornerback Byron Murphy Jr. Former coaches recall meetings with Demmings in which he would lay down freestyle bars over beats for several minutes.
MIT’s human dynamics laboratory would describe him as a “charismatic connector.”
“Relationships are what keep this kid going,” said Marcus Trice, Demmings’ defensive backs coach at John Horn High in Mesquite, Texas. “For him, you have to have a culture that embraces real relationships.”
Demmings’ positive reception in Minnesota has coincided with strong play. Through seven training camp practices, few Vikings players have made more eye-popping plays. Last weekend, Demmings broke up a pass intended for superstar receiver Justin Jefferson, and he swatted away another directed at receiver Tai Felton on Wednesday.
His lateral quickness is perhaps his most impressive on-field feature. The 6-foot-1, 193-pounder starred in high school as a triple jumper. He clocked 4.41 seconds in the 40-yard dash at the NFL Scouting Combine despite soreness in his lower body.
Those athletic characteristics are only relevant if the player also possesses the functionality to use those springs for what his position requires. Demmings does.
The Vikings’ recent history with drafting cornerbacks adds another layer to Demmings’ loud introduction. In 2013, the team picked Xavier Rhodes in the first round. Rhodes became an All-Pro and a shutdown staple. Since then, though, Minnesota has cycled through the following names: Kendall James, Jabari Price, Trae Waynes, Mackensie Alexander, Jack Tocho, Mike Hughes, Kris Boyd, Harrison Hand, Cam Dantzler, Jeff Gladney, Andrew Booth Jr. and Mekhi Blackmon.
Khyree Jackson’s tragic death in the summer of 2024 halted a promising career far too early. Now, Demmings is offering another opportunity for hope.
“Chuck D is a very confident individual,” Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores said. “He’s high energy, (a) great teammate, hard worker. In drills, you see him working his footwork and hand placement, and he tries to apply those things in the group setting. He’s done a good job so far and (has) continued to improve.”
Trice, whose coaching path intersected with Demmings again at Stephen F. Austin, maintains there is still room for growth. Three years ago, for example, Demmings found success at the position based on pure athleticism and feel. Later in his college career, he poured time into receiver tendencies, sharpening his schematic understanding.
Based on how cornerbacks align, receivers release off the line of scrimmage with different techniques. Understanding the opposing receiver’s propensity to move a certain way allows the corner to stay a step ahead, almost like a Major League Baseball hitter projects pitches in particular counts.
Demmings put considerable time and effort into improving this aspect of his game. This intentionality intrigued the Vikings to the degree that they sent defensive backs coach Gerald Alexander to Nacogdoches, Texas, for Demmings’ pro day.
The Vikings validated their interest by drafting him in the fifth round. He did not hide his excitement.
“I am blessed with every breath to be in this position,” Demmings said. “It is literally a privilege. I’m super excited. I’m astounded. And I want to give a big shout-out to everyone who supports the Vikings, who is a part of the staff, the facility, the organization.”
Because Minnesota rosters Murphy and veterans Isaiah Rodgers and James Pierre, Demmings’ immediate path to the field is not clear. At the very least, he has put himself in the conversation as a reliable depth option. In the meantime, he’ll continue making an impact.
Unlike members of MIT’s study, Vikings employees do not wear badges sending signals to data collectors with insights on human communication. This is not necessary for a person such as Demmings.
Watch him interact with anyone from afar, and the details of the conversation are irrelevant. Their reactions tell the entire story.

summary:

FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — When coach Mike Vrabel finally picked up the pieces after the New England Patriots’ Super Bowl loss, left to diagnose what had gone wrong, he kept coming back to one area.
His team needed to run the ball more consistently.

full_text:
The Patriots signed fullback Reggie Gilliam to a three-year contract this offseason in hopes that he would aid the team's running game. Charles Krupa / Associated Press
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — When coach Mike Vrabel finally picked up the pieces after the New England Patriots’ Super Bowl loss, left to diagnose what had gone wrong, he kept coming back to one area.
His team needed to run the ball more consistently.
But getting to that goal wasn’t as easy as a scheme tweak or a change at running back.
They needed a tone setter, someone who would bring the right mentality, but also help create personnel mismatches. They needed, Vrabel determined, to return to the position that the franchise ditched in 2022 after Josh McDaniels left for Las Vegas.
“You have to have a mentality and a mindset to want to run the football,” Vrabel said.
So the Patriots gave Reggie Gilliam the league’s biggest total-value contract for a fullback, a $10.8 million deal over three years.
Gilliam isn’t the draw A.J. Brown is. He doesn’t carry the long-term promise of rookie tight end Eli Raridon or first-round pick Caleb Lomu. But quietly, Gilliam is one of the main reasons for hope that the Patriots offense, already the best in the NFL last season, can improve. Two of the areas that slowed them a year ago were rushing consistency and struggles in the red zone. Gilliam is supposed to help with both.
But his path to this point was a winding one.
Gilliam’s high school football team just outside of Columbus, Ohio, wasn’t any good. It won seven games over his four years. In a football-mad state, no one on his team had even a single star from the recruiting services.
Gilliam played everywhere during those four seasons. But running back was his favorite. He wanted to be LaDainian Tomlinson.
Division I offers never arrived. The best he got was a scout from Toledo reaching out on Twitter to see if he’d be interested in trying to walk on. Not even a formal letter.
Even though tryouts at Toledo went well and earned him a spot on the roster, Gilliam was seventh on the team’s running back depth chart, several rungs behind starter Kareem Hunt. Plus, college life had taken its toll.
Gilliam had gone from 220 pounds in high school to 245 as a freshman. It wasn’t on purpose.
“That freshman 15 is real,” he said.
Gilliam saw the writing on the wall if he stayed at running back. So he asked what he could do to stick with the team and was offered a move to fullback/tight end. He happily accepted, pleased to prolong his football career by a few years.
He played a little as a sophomore, then quite a bit as a junior. The next year, pro scouts came to watch a practice. Toledo produced a few NFL players each year, including Hunt, a third-round pick. But Gilliam was shocked when a scout from the Minnesota Vikings wanted to talk to him.
“I was like, ‘ Me ?’” Gilliam said. “I’ve got a shot at the NFL?! You’re not just here to see these other guys?”
Gilliam participated in some post-college all-star events to try to make an impression. His pre-draft measurements helped. Gilliam has 34-inch arms, longer than four of the Patriots’ five starting offensive linemen. It helps him latch onto would-be tacklers more easily. (“I’m so glad you mentioned that,” Gilliam said with a laugh. “Make sure you tell everybody you know. Because there’s a stigma that running backs and fullbacks have stubby arms.”)
Still, only one team seemed to be pursuing Gilliam. In the weeks before the draft, the Baltimore Ravens made their interest known. Scouts hit up Gilliam every other day. Then-coach John Harbaugh personally called Gilliam. They sent care packages full of Ravens gear so he’d have something to wear after they drafted him.
Gilliam was over the moon. His parents were living in Baltimore at the time. He made plans for the future, even setting up a place to live in their house during training camp to save money.
In the sixth round, Gilliam put on his Ravens hat. It was time. But he watched as they selected a wide receiver.
He was disappointed, but the seventh round came around quickly. When the Ravens were on the clock again, Gilliam’s parents took out their phones to record the big moment. They watched as Baltimore picked a safety.
“I’m calling my agent like, ‘What the hell happened?’” Gilliam said. “Was John Harbaugh blowing smoke up my ass? He’s like, ‘Yeah that happens with everyone.’”
After the draft, Gilliam had three offers: the Vikings, Giants and Bills. He Googled each team’s roster. All three had fullbacks already, but the Bills had the oldest one in 31-year-old Patrick DiMarco. So Gilliam chose Buffalo.
But that was 2020. The COVID-19 pandemic scrapped rookie minicamp and spring practices. Gilliam studied virtually with assistant coaches. It was impossible to learn everything about where he needed to be on the field.
Gilliam figured that was fine. DiMarco would get most of the snaps. Gilliam had time to learn and develop.
At the first padded practice in training camp, DiMarco broke his neck.
“And I’m like, holy s—, this is real now,” Gilliam said.
Gilliam’s next practice went well. Same for the one after that. The Bills never brought in another fullback to compete with him. But Gilliam still didn’t know whether he’d make the team. So he asked teammates how cutdown day worked.
The deadline for cuts was 4 p.m. ET, he was told. If you get called into the facility, that’s a bad sign. If you don’t get a call, you made it.
Gilliam kept his phone on loud. When 4 p.m. arrived without a call, Gilliam assumed they must’ve forgotten to call. He stared at his phone. He left it on loud when he went to bed that night so he wouldn’t miss the call when the team realized its mistake.
He drove his 2014 Dodge Charger into the facility at 7:30 the next morning, a little early for the 8 a.m. team meeting. When he pulled in, he saw a swarm of players already heading out. He panicked. He’d just made the team, and now he was missing his first meeting?
“I’m like, ‘I’m definitely going to be cut now,'” Gilliam said.
He ran inside and saw veteran players lounging. Confused, he asked what that 7:30 meeting was about and why so many players were already leaving.
“They were like, ‘Oh, that’s the group of guys that got cut,’” Gilliam said.
At 8 a.m., Gilliam was given the news in a team meeting. He had made the roster.
“I’m trying to keep my composure, but I’m like, ‘Holy s—, you actually made the team!'” he said.
The nature of the position and his background never allowed for an exhale or a moment where he felt like a no-doubt NFL player. The following training camp, he wondered if he’d make the team. Same for the next year.
Now, he’s entering Year 7. That feeling still hasn’t gone away.
“I know I signed a three-year contract, but that doesn’t mean my spot is guaranteed,” Gilliam said.
What comes next are the interesting parts. He joined a Patriots offense that led the AFC in expected points added per play last season. And he’s supposed to help make them better.
He’ll be tasked with creating more holes for running backs Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson and helping give the team more of a running identity.
But it’s also part of a trend around the league to use fullbacks to create mismatches. If the Patriots put Gilliam on the field alongside a running back, tight end and two wide receivers (21 personnel), they can pretty much dictate that the defense will play with three linebackers and stack the box. That makes the Pats more susceptible to play action and the passing game, which is where New England thrives.
Then, if teams swap in an extra defensive back to counter that, the Pats can use Gilliam as a lead blocker to hammer the defense on the ground for consistent gains (which they weren’t great at a year ago).
“Fullbacks,” Gilliam said, “are the hybrids now.”

full_text:
Joe Brady and Josh Allen hope to knock down the proverbial wall en route to the Super Bowl this season. Bryan Bennett / Getty Images
The obvious connection between New Orleans and Buffalo dates back more than 60 years.
As popular — but perhaps not entirely true — legend has it, Buffalo wings were invented at the Anchor Bar in 1964, when the owner doused some chicken parts with Frank’s RedHot Sauce and served them up with celery and a side of bleu cheese dressing.
This offseason, the Buffalo Bills decided to cook up another north-south collaboration.
And they laid it on thick.
Since the day the Bills named Joe Brady head coach, they have promoted his relationships with former New Orleans Saints coach Sean Payton and quarterback Drew Brees, who will be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Saturday.
“I got a master’s degree at Penn State, but I got a doctorate in New Orleans,” was a line Brady said the day he was introduced as the Bills’ new head coach and which he repeated often along the national media circuit.
While finishing his master’s degree in educational leadership at Penn State, Brady entered the NFL as a Saints offensive assistant in 2017 and 2018 before joining LSU’s staff as passing game coordinator and helping the Tigers win the 2019 national championship. It was a solid curriculum vitae for the NFL’s youngest head coach.
But would it be good enough for Buffalo to recreate New Orleans’ syllabus?
Brees was a deity in New Orleans, and by the time he retired, he held the NFL record for career passing yards and ranked second in touchdown passes and completion percentage. Yet during Brees’ 15 years there, New Orleans won only one Super Bowl (2009). It never returned to the big game, and failed to make the postseason six times.
The club had so much money committed to its franchise quarterback that it struggled to assemble a comprehensive roster. The Saints went 7-9 four times during a five-year span in which Brees led the NFL in passing yards four times, averaging 5,074 yards and 37 TDs per season.
Then again, maybe a single Lombardi Trophy would satisfy Bills fans.
Bobby Hebert didn’t take the classes, but he knows all the professors and has dissected the lessons.
“Under Drew Brees and Sean Payton, they should have won or gone to at least three Super Bowls,” said Hebert, the legendary Saints quarterback from Cut Off, La.
“I guess you can say they underachieved. It just goes to show how hard it is to win the Super Bowl, the ultimate. The Bills better take advantage of Josh Allen.”
Early this offseason, Brady repeatedly mentioned being “from the Sean Payton tree.” The comment entered a pantheon of “Hey, did you know” jokes among local reporters alongside former Bills overachievers Ryan Fitzpatrick attending Harvard and Chris Hogan starting out as a lacrosse player.
“Look, I was a coaching assistant, right?” Brady said. “I was bottom of the barrel, sleeping at the office, loving life. But I got an opportunity to learn everything from him, and there’s no way in hell I’d be sitting in this chair right now if I didn’t get that opportunity to be his coaching assistant.”
Brady said he’s going to keep calling plays because he has seen Payton be successful at it. Brady hired two coordinators away from Payton, who has been the Denver Broncos’ coach since 2023. The first was offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael, who also spent 14 seasons with Payton and the Saints, followed by defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. Brady’s senior adviser, former head coach John Fox, was the New York Giants’ defensive coordinator in 2001 and 2002 when Payton was their offensive coordinator.
“But the biggest thing that I learned along the way,” said Brady, “is that if I’m not myself, it’s not going to work. If I try to just, hey, pick up, ‘Oh, this is what Coach Payton did’ and take it somewhere else, that’s not going to work. That’s important, that I have to be me, and I think the great coaches that I’ve been around have been comfortable in who they are.”
Brady made an impression on Brees, who said he “wasn’t surprised” when Brady left New Orleans and won a national title on LSU’s staff, working with future NFL stars Joe Burrow, Justin Jefferson and Ja’Marr Chase. After that amazing season, at just 30 years old, Brady began interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs.
“I think his demeanor, his personality is one that, as a quarterback, you really feel like you can relate to him,” Brees said. “He’s really built the system around the guys that he has. He’s going to be able to do a lot of creative, innovative stuff there.
“Sean was brilliant in so many ways. He was brilliant in the way he narrowed the focus for the team week in and week out. He was brilliant in the way that he managed the coaching staff and helped develop his coaches to go on and be play callers and head coaches elsewhere. A lot of guys who have coached under Sean Payton would give him a lot of credit for a lot of things and say they learned a whole lot.
“And, back in those days, Joe Brady probably was supporting Pete Carmichael in ways that he is probably now supporting Joe.”
Hebert knew Brady way back when.
Hebert, who turns 66 this month, remains a New Orleans fixture. He has been immersed in Saints and LSU football as a sportscaster there for 25 years. His Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame bio calls him “the most successful quarterback in team history,” greater than Saints icon Archie Manning, until Brees came along. Hebert was born on the bayou. He was a state-championship high school teammate and Northwestern State roommate with — and is a cousin of — Brady’s LSU boss, Ed Orgeron.
“People don’t realize: Joe Brady gets a lot of credit, but he wasn’t calling the plays,” Hebert said. “Brady had a lot of input, but Steve Ensminger was the one really running that LSU offense when they were having the greatest season ever in college football.
“What Joe Brady would do is help out Ensminger in the red zone and with certain plays and on third down. Ensminger would, for Brady to get his feet wet, let him call a few series. But Ensminger is a humble man, so he doesn’t demand the credit he deserves.”
That said, Hebert predicted Brady will prove to be a good hire for Buffalo. The “Cajun Cannon” noted that Brady’s learning curve was aided by a disappointing-but-educational stint as the Carolina Panthers’ offensive coordinator and then by his re-emergence with Allen and the Bills. Hebert said he sees many positive similarities between Brady and young Saints coach Kellen Moore.
As for any Saints redux, Hebert avoided that nasty NFL voodoo.
“The year they won the Super Bowl, that wasn’t even the Saints’ best team,” Hebert said. “The best team was in 2011. They became the new Greatest Show on Turf, better than those Rams teams. They were No. 1 in a number of offensive categories.”
That Saints team was upset by the San Francisco 49ers in the second round. New Orleans surrendered a 17-point lead in the second quarter and committed five turnovers, but took a pair of leads within the final five minutes, the last with 1:37 left. They didn’t survive.
Then, there was the “NOLA No-Call” at the end of the 2018 NFC Championship Game.
“Look at Dan Marino: ‘Oh, he’s just a rookie, he’ll be back.’ Look at Joe Burrow, who got there and lost and now might never get back,” Hebert said. “It’s hard.”
Despite having an all-time great at the most critical position for 15 years, the Saints’ front office struggled infamously with the salary cap, frequently cutting serviceable veterans and constantly restructuring contracts to comply. When they signed Bills left guard David Edwards in March for $61 million over four years, stunned media and fans noted the deal included no void years , ubiquitous since long before Brees retired after the 2020 season.

full_text:
Odell Beckham Jr. looks like he still has juice, but will it be enough for him to beat out his competition? Ryan Hunt / Getty Images
WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants overhauled their wide receiver corps this offseason, signing a handful of high-profile veterans (Odell Beckham Jr., Darnell Mooney, Calvin Austin III, JuJu Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios) and trading up in the third round for Malachi Fields. Still, everything hinges on the health of top returning receiver Malik Nabers.
While Nabers continues his recovery from a torn ACL and meniscus, the rest of the depth chart is wide open. Nabers’ absence has allowed a crowd of complementary pieces to vie for roles early in training camp. Here’s a player-by-player look at one of the most intriguing positions on the roster:
Nabers has had a steady workload since the start of training camp, participating in individual drills, running routes on air and jogging through plays in install periods most days. Nabers is moving well, even if he still hasn’t fully cut it loose. The Giants could ramp up Nabers more, but they have structured everything toward having him ready for the Sept. 13 opener against the Dallas Cowboys. It wouldn’t be a surprise if Nabers starts to work in team periods next week, which would be an important checkpoint in his comeback.
Fields has demonstrated an ability to make plays downfield, which could be his primary role as a rookie. Unlike Jalin Hyatt, whose speed made him a deep threat exclusively, the 6-foot-4, 222-pound Fields has the size to run underneath routes and use his physicality to make contested catches. With the Giants expected to lean heavily on two-tight end packages, Fields has made an early claim for the No. 2 receiver spot opposite Nabers.
Shades of Michael Pittman, but must work on expanding his route tree.
Austin was the most impressive wide receiver in the spring. That hasn’t carried over to the start of camp, but he’s still the team’s top slot option. The slot receiver won’t be featured nearly as much in this offense as it was when Wan’Dale Robinson was racking up 140 targets per season. But even the teams that employ big personnel the most use three-receiver sets when trailing and running two-minute drills. That means Austin will have a role, and he should get the short targets Robinson once received in New York.
Slayton isn’t going anywhere due to his contract, but there are no assurances about his role. Slayton dealt with a sports hernia last season and had surgery in the spring. There’s hope he’ll bounce back now that he’s healthy, but he’s had a quiet start to camp as he works his way back into shape.
Mooney feels a bit like the new Slayton. Mooney’s warts have been overlooked because fans don’t have a history with him, but he’s had a similarly inconsistent career. Mooney hasn’t stood out this offseason, as the 5-foot-11, 177-pounder’s stature limits his impact. Mooney is at his best on the deep crossers that offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s scheme features.
The No. 6 wide receiver doesn’t necessarily have to play special teams, but Beckham will need to produce more this summer to justify carrying him as a depth receiver. Beckham looks like he still has juice, and that showed up Wednesday in his best practice of camp. The delay in signing Beckham in the spring involved both sides discussing the possibility his comeback bid falls short. Beckham will need to raise his play and maintain it to avoid that fate.
Camp production by veteran slot receivers, especially with the second team, can be misleading. A savvy veteran like Berrios has a distinct advantage going up against inexperienced/weak slot corners, and he has exploited that in camp. Still, his production can’t be ignored. Berrios’ return ability gives him true game-day value. He profiles as a replacement for Gunner Olszewski, who tore an Achilles tendon in the spring.
Special teams is the path to a roster spot for Cambre, but his impressive receiving in camp is aiding his bid. Harbaugh said Cambre is “making a move,” and “he’s got our attention.” Those are strong statements about a second-year receiver who signed as an undrafted rookie last year. There are minimal offensive snaps available for the sixth wide receiver. Meanwhile, Cambre averaged 12.7 special teams snaps in seven games last season, so he could provide more value than other receivers vying for the final spot.
Smith-Schuster had the most production in the spring of the three wide receivers signed June 1. But he’s been quiet in camp, missing practice on Tuesday due to knee swelling. Smith-Schuster doesn’t play special teams, so he’ll need to pick it up soon to make a serious push for a roster spot.
A year ago, optimists held out hope Hyatt would still develop. He is now an afterthought, even though he has made a few plays this offseason. If the Giants felt good about Hyatt, they wouldn’t have added so many veteran wide receivers this offseason. The Giants hung onto Hyatt as a healthy scratch for much of last season to avoid cutting a third-round pick. They can’t be worried about those optics anymore, and Hyatt should be craving a fresh start at this point.
It speaks to the pieces the Giants have added at wide receiver that Hodgins has fallen so far down the depth chart. Hodgins hasn’t made any plays in camp to get into the mix. Hodgins has never played special teams, which is a major impediment to his chances. He is an ideal vet to stash on the practice squad.
The Berrios signing was a major blow to Gipson’s chances of making the roster. If the Giants viewed Gipson as a viable receiver/returner, they likely wouldn’t have signed Berrios immediately after Olszewski’s injury.
It’s impossible to see a path to a roster spot for Miller. He has to be hoping to land on the practice squad, but even that will be tough with so much competition for the final roster spots.

title: Cam Ward and Brian Daboll's fast-developing bond could determine Titans' success Says Ward: "We’re both aggressive. We’re both reckless. We both have to be tamed at times. We're actually the same person." Mike Jones
summary:
